analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 35.5% of educational services firms (NAICS 61) reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 33.8% in the prior period. The survey question asks whether the business used AI in that window, and the figure covers the educational services sector as a whole.

The Department of Education's AI use-case inventory shows a range of administrative and technical applications. It lists CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly for writing refinement; Otter.AI for transcription of meetings, interviews, and lectures; and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, returning R code for data analysis, converting county names to FIPS codes, creating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies, and writing job descriptions.

The Department of Education has also issued federal AI guidance that frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education. Its inventory includes providing fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention methods, which points to security and misuse concerns in deployment. The excerpt does not detail specific policy provisions for schools, but the guidance is positioned as covering innovation and risk management.

The World of AI's course catalog lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, with 3 offering public companion code. Four are university graduate courses with public materials: Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191. The rest come from industry providers including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy. Only fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero, and MIT's 6.S191 list public code repositories. The catalog does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy, including EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning, but the excerpt provides no specific funding or market size figures. None of the source excerpts report ROI evidence from education AI deployments. A reader deciding whether to deploy should note that adoption is measurable and rising, federal guidance exists, and training options are catalogued, but hard evidence on returns and vendor concentration is not present in these sources.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
